title: The profile picture I stopped editing

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Today we are talking about online identity with student photographer Eva Morgan. Eva, you recently stopped heavily editing your profile pictures. Why?

segments.speaker: Eva
segments.text: I realized I was spending more time adjusting the picture than deciding whether I actually liked the moment it showed. I would brighten my skin, change the background and remove tiny details that nobody else would probably notice.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Did the edited pictures feel dishonest?

segments.speaker: Eva
segments.text: Not exactly. Choosing a flattering photo is normal. The problem was that I had started judging ordinary photos as failures. If a picture did not look polished enough for my profile, I felt as if the experience itself had somehow been less successful.

segments.speaker: Eva
segments.text: I still crop images and correct obvious lighting problems, but I use a simple rule: I should still recognize the person and place I remember. I also post fewer pictures. That sounds like a small change, but it makes the account feel more like a record of my life and less like a performance I have to maintain.

questions.prompt: What made Eva question her editing habits?
options: She lost access to editing software.
She spent more time editing than thinking about the memory itself.
Her school banned social media.
Her friends stopped taking photographs.
questions.explanationJa: 写真そのものより編集に時間をかけていることに気づいたのがきっかけです。

questions.prompt: Give two examples of changes Eva used to make to profile pictures.
markscheme: She brightened her skin and/or adjusted lighting.
She changed the background and/or removed small details.
questions.explanationJa: skinの明るさ、background、細かな不要物などを編集していました。

questions.prompt: What was the main problem for Eva?
options: All edited photos felt completely fake.
She began treating ordinary photos and experiences as inadequate.
She could no longer remember where pictures were taken.
She wanted to become a professional model.
questions.explanationJa: 普通の写真まで失敗のように感じ、経験そのものの価値まで下げて考えるようになった点です。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO things Eva still allows herself to do.
options: Crop an image
Replace the people in a photo
Correct obvious lighting problems
Change every background
Remove any feature she dislikes
questions.explanationJa: cropと明らかなlighting correctionは今も行います。

questions.prompt: Eva wants her account to feel more like a record of her life and less like a ________.
questions.explanationJa: 常に見せ方を作るperformanceではなく、生活のrecordにしたいと述べます。

questions.prompt: Which attitude best describes Eva now?
options: She rejects all image editing.
She uses limited editing while trying to preserve a recognizable reality.
She believes online identity should be completely anonymous.
She wants to post as many pictures as possible.
questions.explanationJa: 編集を全面否定せず、現実とのつながりを残す範囲に限定しています。

title: The language I nearly stopped speaking

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: When I was twelve, I started answering my grandmother in English even when she spoke to me in Tagalog. I understood her perfectly, but English was faster for me and it was the language I used at school.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: For a while nobody complained. Then I noticed that our conversations were becoming shorter. My grandmother could speak English, but jokes, family stories and small expressions came more naturally to her in Tagalog. By choosing convenience, I was quietly reducing the range of things we talked about.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: I decided to change one habit rather than make a dramatic promise. During Sunday lunch, I would answer in Tagalog even if I had to pause or ask for a word. At first I sounded slow and childish. That was uncomfortable, especially because I knew what I wanted to say but could not always say it elegantly.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: After several months the pauses became shorter. More importantly, my grandmother started telling longer stories again. I still use English most of the day, and I do not think one language makes me more authentic than another. What matters is that I no longer confuse fluency with the only kind of connection worth keeping.

questions.prompt: Why did the speaker begin replying in English?
options: Her grandmother requested it.
English was faster and used at school.
She had forgotten all Tagalog.
She wanted to move abroad.
questions.explanationJa: schoolで使うEnglishの方が速く答えられたためです。

questions.prompt: Give two things that became harder to share when the conversations shifted to English.
markscheme: Family stories and/or longer, more natural conversation.
questions.explanationJa: jokes、family stories、細かな表現などが共有しにくくなりました。

questions.prompt: At first, speaking Tagalog at Sunday lunch made the speaker feel slow and ________.
questions.explanationJa: 自分の話し方がslow and childishに感じられたと述べています。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO changes that happened after several months.
options: The pauses became shorter.
The family stopped using English.
The grandmother told longer stories again.
The speaker became a professional translator.
Sunday lunch ended.
questions.explanationJa: pauseが短くなり、grandmotherのstoriesも長くなりました。

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about authenticity?
options: Only Tagalog represents the real self.
Only English represents the real self.
Neither language automatically makes the speaker more authentic.
Authenticity depends on speaking without pauses.
questions.explanationJa: どちらか一方だけが本当の自分を表すとは考えていません。

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the essay?
options: To argue that bilingual people should avoid English
To show how language choice can affect family connection and identity
To teach Tagalog grammar
To criticize the speaker's school
questions.explanationJa: language choiceがfamily connectionとidentityに与える影響が中心です。

title: Dress codes and who gets to belong

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: Our panel is discussing dress codes for school events. Jordan, you support having some rules.

segments.speaker: Jordan
segments.text: Yes. A formal event can have a shared atmosphere, and basic expectations help people know what is appropriate. My concern is not with having any rule at all; it is with rules that assume everyone owns the same kind of clothing.

segments.speaker: Leila
segments.text: Gendered wording. If one list tells boys to wear suits and another tells girls to wear dresses, students who do not identify with those categories may feel that the school has already decided how they should present themselves.

segments.speaker: Theo
segments.text: Cost. A rule can sound neutral but still exclude someone if the approved clothes are expensive. Schools could describe the level of formality instead of naming specific items, and they could offer a borrowing rail or second-hand options.

segments.speaker: Jordan
segments.text: I agree. 'Smart and safe' is more useful than a long list of exact clothes. It gives guidance without pretending that one style is the only respectable one.

segments.speaker: Leila
segments.text: And any safety restriction should be explained. Students are more likely to accept a limit if they understand the reason rather than being told that a particular look is simply inappropriate.

segments.speaker: Moderator
segments.text: So the common ground is that a dress code can guide an event, but it should avoid unnecessary assumptions about gender, money and respectability.

options: No dress rules at all
Basic shared expectations without assuming everyone owns the same clothes
Only expensive formal clothing
Separate events for different styles
questions.explanationJa: 基本的なexpectationは認めつつ、所有する服を一律に想定することには反対です。

questions.prompt: Give two concerns raised about traditional dress-code wording.
markscheme: Gendered lists can exclude students who do not identify with the assumed categories.
Specific approved clothing can create financial barriers / cost pressure.
questions.explanationJa: gender assumptionとcostが主な問題です。

options: Cancel formal events
Describe the level of formality instead of naming exact items
Require school uniforms at every event
Let teachers choose each student's clothes
questions.explanationJa: specific itemではなくformalityのlevelを示す方法を提案します。

questions.prompt: Choose TWO practical ideas suggested by the speakers.
options: A borrowing rail or second-hand options
Explaining the reason for safety restrictions
Banning all accessories
Requiring one approved shop
Using different rules for every student
questions.explanationJa: borrow/second-handとsafety ruleの理由説明が提案されています。

questions.prompt: Matching task: Match the speaker to the main concern: Leila and Theo.
markscheme: Leila — gendered assumptions / how students are expected to present themselves.
Theo — cost / financial access to approved clothing.
questions.explanationJa: Leilaはgender、Theoはcostを中心に話しています。

questions.prompt: What is the moderator's purpose in the final sentence?
options: To declare one speaker the winner
To summarize the shared position and its limits
To introduce a new dress rule
To argue that formal events are unnecessary
questions.explanationJa: 共通点をまとめ、dress codeのあり方を整理しています。
